doc.title: Scott Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe,Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: The contrabass album and bass sax discography
summary: He describes the new record's personnel and instruments, and his brother's bass sax discography.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: So what’s the context of the record you’re going to record? Did you use a rhythm section?
You mean the record that’s coming out?

Yeah that’s already been recorded. That’s coming out next week I think. It’s a rhythm section, it’s a couple of extra horns on some of the tracks. Dan Barrett’s on it, my brother David plays cornet and trumpet on maybe half of it. And the contrabass is on two cuts and the rest, there’s a lot of bass sax, there’s some sarrousaphone and tenor, C melody and so on. I didn’t play any brass on this record.
But you do play brass too.

Well that’s interesting. I suppose in some sense it’s good to specialize in those kind of things because you have less competition. How many guys around play bass sax? And wasn’t there a bass saxophone on a Paul Simon record, “Graceland?” I remember seeing someone playing the bass sax, just on that one tune.
I don’t know. I don’t know too much about pop music.
And I recognized the name too — there’s one other guy that does it occasionally. I can’t think of it at the moment.

Well it’s possible. My brother is working on a discography of the bass saxophone. He’s been doing it for years, and he’s dug up a lot of incredibly obscure items. And there’s some classical things, shows and movie music and different things that you wouldn’t necessarily know about. There’s a lot of stuff out there besides the Adrian Rollini and Spencer Clark stuff.
